#6895. A New Exhibition Celebrates the Mantilla in Fashion and Art

The garment finally gets its due credit at The Hispanic Society Museum & Library.

Few garments have been as imitated, reinterpreted, and misunderstood as the mantilla. The iconic lace veil with Spanish roots has endured for centuries. What started as an object traditionally worn for ceremonies has had a renaissance via Madonna, Rosalía, and Dolce & Gabbana, just to name a few. That’s just one of the reasons why The Hispanic Society Museum & Library in New York is opening its new exhibition “Mantilla: Fashion Unveiled” beginning November 20. The museum calls the mantilla the “most distinctive garment in Spanish women’s fashion with origins dating to the 16th century.” Curated by Spanish-born scholar Carlos Usabiaga López, the show merges fashion, art, and archival material to shine a light on an iconic garment that has been donned on screen, on runways, and on red carpets for generations.

“The understanding of the mantilla in all its complexity is often limited, either by a superficial reading of the symbol itself or by its association with an old-fashioned, rather conservative image of Spain,” López tells ELLE. “This exhibition challenges the perception of the mantilla as an anachronistic relic of the past and reclaims its continued cultural relevance and subversive potential. From Spanish countercultural movements such as ‘La Movida Madrileña’ to drag performance, the mantilla has repeatedly been appropriated and reimagined in ways that reveal its capacity to carry new meanings.”

The exhibition is the second installment in the Hispanic Society’s multiyear fashion initiative, which focuses on reinterpreting its own renowned collection through a new lens. The museum was founded in 1903 by American philanthropist Archer Milton Huntington and has many visual examples of the garment, including Francisco Goya’s famed portrait of María del Pilar Teresa Cayetana de Silva y Álvarez de Toledo, the 13th Duchess of Alba (1762–1802). “By bringing together works of art, fashion, and material culture, the iconography of the mantilla activates a collection of such an extraordinary diversity, through unexpected dialogues between the museum’s different departments and international loans,” adds López.

The new exhibition pulls from many cultural moments new and old, including the “Spanish Craze,” which was a period of cultural fascination with Spain in the United States spanning 1890 to 1930. “During this period, the mantilla became part of a highly recognizable visual language through which Spain was imagined and represented in America,” says López. “Spanish performers who travelled to the United States achieved remarkable success: Raquel Meller, for instance, appeared on the cover of Time magazine in 1926, while Concha Piquer starred in From Far Seville (1923).” He also points to the reinterpretation of the mantilla in The Devil Is a Woman (1935), starring Marlene Dietrich.

Fashion naturally plays a role in the show, especially through the imagination of emerging designers, like Arturo Obegero. “Throughout the history of fashion, major designers such as Cristóbal Balenciaga and Óscar de la Renta have drawn inspiration from this [Spanish] visual language, including the mantilla,” adds López. “However, it was a curatorial decision to bring contemporary designers, including emerging voices, into direct conversation with the masterpieces in order to make justice to the mantilla’s enduring influence on fashion to this day.”

The mantilla has been loved (and reinvented) in contemporary fashion at least since the 1940s, when it appeared in numerous fashion magazines. Today, the references are endless and people of all cultures and backgrounds are embracing it. “I think there is something particularly beautiful about the fact that those who have historically been excluded from the dominant narrative, who may have felt unrepresented or even oppressed by these national symbols, can now feel encouraged to revisit this folklore and expand its boundaries to make room for others to do the same,” says López. As the exhibition makes clear, the mantilla’s compelling story is still unfolding.

“Mantilla: Fashion Unveiled” is on view at The Hispanic Society Museum & Library from Nov. 20, 2026, through March 28, 2027.

#6893. Pride and Prejudice’s Rufus Sewell Is the Most Dashing Man on Television

It’s possible that Rufus Sewell is having too much fun right now. Between playing morally ambiguous Vice President (and husband to the U.S. Ambassador to the Court of St. James’s) Hal Wyler in Netflix’s frothy, prestige-y series The Diplomat and the beloved but deeply flawed Mr. Bennet in the streamer’s upcoming adaptation of Pride and Prejudice, he’s cornered the market on lovable rascals. He thrives on “exercises in gray” and relishes “when it goes wrong” for a character. “It’s the opposite of what you want in life,” he tells me. “You want drama, you want mistakes.” These roles offer plenty of both.

Wyler, of The Diplomat, is navigating how to work with the increasingly autocratic and bloody-minded President Grace Penn (Allison Janney) thousands of miles away from his wife Kate (Keri Russell), who is starting to exhibit some of his own manipulative behaviors she claims to abhor. Two centuries prior, Mr. Bennet is reckoning not with geopolitical crises and egomaniacal heads of state, but with the challenges his wife faces in marrying off five eligible, if dowry-poor, daughters.

Sewell sat down for a long chat with GQ about the two series, the value of blending high silliness with high stakes in the same scene, and how bodily functions are an under-appreciated key to unlocking a character’s specificity.

Rufus Sewell: The interesting question for me, for the second half of the season, was how much is Hal truly aware of everything that Kate and everyone else are noticing and concerned about with Grace's behavior. How much does he see? How much is he choosing to pretend not to see in order to stay in the room? He's always believed that access is all, but how much do you compromise in order to stay in the room? Where’s the point when you realize you stayed in the room too long without saying anything, and the moment’s passed, and you are just an accomplice? I found it very difficult to play his seeming unctuousness and obsequiousness with Grace this season, and to not be trying to protect my character in the wrong way, because I felt he was failing.

He’s overestimated his ability to effect change with Grace. Hal was prepared to appear to be supporting her, when he believed in his ability to steer her in a better direction, and I think he goes past that point. When I read the final episode script and saw where he ends up walking out, it gave me the courage to really lean into how much he goes wrong, by his own standards earlier in the season. He begins to lose his way in a way that he never has done before. But I embraced it, knowing that the real gift of the part was getting to play him going wrong and then seemingly correcting himself. We actually shot a speech that he made, just to give us a sense of where the scene was headed and for me to know how to play it. They might end up using some of it in the next season, or they could end up completely changing what was written. Hal coming out of the summit is a momentous decision in terms of what that does for the future and I've got no idea what’s next—I can't wait to start filming season five to find out.

I was always shocked when this show was described as a thriller because I always thought it was a kind of romantic sex comedy with extremely high stakes, because what it reminded me of firstly was some of the comedy of divorce screwball films of the 1940s. The characters may be divorced after a very tempestuous relationship, but they’re interlinked in a way that can never be undone. There's a romance to all of that history.

The other thing that it reminded me of was the kind of films that were made in the '70s—French films where halfway through an argument one of the characters would sit down on the toilet, you know what I mean? The people inside these films remind you of your own relationships. Your long-term relationship might not go to the same extremes, it might not be in the same setting, but I think people are people. What I love about their relationship is their shared wonkiness, and the getting into the nitty-gritty of the politics and taking someone down and hatching a plot whilst fighting over pastries and getting crumbs on the bed—all of that is part of their foreplay.

That is what the show is about, as far as I'm concerned. These are people who wear suits that might stand at a lectern and be on TV, but the fact is, how do you scratch an itch? Do you smell? Do you need to go to the toilet? These are the things that the script leans into a lot, and it might put some people off, but I don't care about that. That's the thing that makes it feel real, and it's so refreshing to play.

He'll flirt with anyone. We all know people like this. It's not even necessarily sexual, he just engages with people on that level and it's a natural thing for him.

I would say Hal’s flirtatiousness being a problem is open for debate, because a lot of what we understand of him is via Kate’s descriptions of him and his behavior. I can and often do see it in a different way. Part of the story of seasons three and four is Kate’s realization that a lot of stuff she thought of as his personality was in fact the mantle of the job that he'd taken on, because we see her doing the same kinds of things now that she is an ambassador. They both have a lot of the same qualities. They're both killers in a sense, and it's been very convenient for her and great for the show for her to introduce the public to Hal through her descriptions. And yet, every time it seems like he's changed character, in fact, it is revealing something from a different perspective.

We learned pretty early on that we were going to be doing some very, very long scenes, and we were given the advantage of seeing the scenes very early so we could slowly gestate the performances. We needed that because Windsor Castle in the show was comprised of several different buildings and locations, some of them with oceans between them, so we’d be shooting some parts the next day, and other bits in four months’ time.

Especially with a two-hander, with such long takes, you can go in and out of being relaxed, unrelaxed, free, slightly bound, and actually you get to the point where you stop worrying about it. It's like being on stage, because you end up too tired to be bad all the time and end up inhabiting the moment and things just happen. I love that all of it was a surprise to us.

I think what is most important in this particular iteration of the relationship between Mr. and Mrs. Bennet is that he comes to realize which ways he's failed his daughters. When Mrs. Bennet says to him in this version, it's easy for you to say that I’m silly or frivolous, but you try being a woman at this age with no means—this is the fight of their lives that he is making these jokes about. And yes, of course he's funny and right in certain ways, but he's also guilty of negligence of his family for the sake of an easy life for himself. The reason they have no money is that so much money has been spent on bonnets. Money could have been saved, but in order to have a quiet life, he's ducked out of fights in order to avoid responsibility.

Exactly. It was a gift in this role to have that moment when he feels that, admits that, and gets to be slightly humbled in this idea of himself that he's been cultivating. He didn’t actively or consciously avoid having this revelation, but that’s the effect of staying in his study, and now he’s facing the consequences. To use very modern terms, he has a revelation of what his pattern has been. It made sense!

One could be forgiven for thinking that Mr. and Mrs. Bennet are two people that used to be attracted to each other and now have nothing in common and don't like each other. I think it's born out in the book, though, the idea that there is still a love there, and especially a shared humor between them, and a bit of a spark remains.

I love the fact that we get to get drunk together and stuff like that. Olivia Colman and I worked on The Father together a few years ago with Anthony Hopkins, which was a very different kind of gig, but as is often the case with things that are very heavy and intense, we had a hoot doing it. I loved working with her, and was very excited about the chance to work with her again. I love the scenes between Mr. Bennet and Mrs. Bennet. They were such a treat for us.

#6891. 25 Best Airbnbs in Paris 2026 for a Stylish Sojourn in the City of Light

When you book something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

There are two sorts of Parisian holidays. The first, an exercise in blissful escapism, where luxury hotels, gallery hopping, and lazy apéros à la terrasse all help you lean into the romantic undercurrent of the city. The second, an exercise in make-believe: You would not be the first person to plot a move to Paris halfway through your stay there, earmarking local boulangeries and wine shops as favorites and spending mornings chit-chatting with market vendors. If you lean toward the latter experience, this is where the best Airbnbs in Paris enter the picture. After all, what better way to cosplay a Parisienne than via a cozy flat of your own (albeit a temporary one)?

Our edit is an evolving one—there’s no shortage of stately Haussmann buildings available for rent—grouped by arrondissement. (There are 20 total, and while we haven’t hit on all of them, the below list includes several of the most popular for visitors.) Each spot has its own distinct flair, depending on what sort of Parisian you wish to embody. The chichi traveler with high-brow tastes will love the classic charm of the Left Bank; the arty fashion-lover will prefer the cozy studios of the Marais (as well as its proximity to some of the best vintage shops); the low-key bohemian will find respite in the hills of Montmarte, above the city’s lights. Grand architecture and bistro balconies, you’ll be glad to discover, have no loyalty to any particular arrondissement. They’re all good; you really can’t go wrong.

For anyone planning a trip to the City of Light, consider the roundup of properties ahead for a true immersive experience in one of the most stylish cities on the planet.

For a grand apartment right in the middle of the historical center, book this ornate Airbnb. Travelers looking to see all the sights will appreciate its proximity to the Palais Royal, Centre Pompidou, and the Louvre; it’s also around the corner from the Les Halles shopping center, where you’ll find both great restaurants (Le Petit Bouillon Pharamond is a nice option for an affordable lunch and gorgeous interiors) and little shops (E. Dehillerin, Julia Child’s much-frequented kitchenware store, is a must). The home itself is no less impressive—high ceilings with crown molding, antique gilded mirrors, and parquet floors run throughout.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer, indoor fireplace, long-term stays allowed, elevator

Exposed beams and parquet flooring set the scene for this typically charming Parisian apartment. There’s lots of space for making yourself right at home, including a stunning balcony that sits atop Rue de Rivoli so you’ll feel like you’re right in the middle of everything as you sip your morning espresso while mapping out the day’s itinerary. Then there’s the location: If it’s your first time visiting Paris, the fact that the Louvre museum, the Centre Pompidou, and the Seine are all within walking distance will be a massive bonus. Leave the complicated commutes for your sophomore outing; this home lets you walk everywhere.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathrooms; sleeps 4

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, blackout shades, Devialet Bluetooth sound system, television, air conditioning, kitchen, dishwasher, espresso machine, balcony, housekeeping available at a cost

This sun-drenched two-bedroom near the Seine opens with a grand, golden-colored lobby, complete with a spiral staircase and tile floors. Upstairs, the duplex has lots of space to stretch out, from a dining table that doubles as a workspace to a bright living room to a small balcony. You’ll have both the fifth and sixth floors—but as there’s no elevator, prepare to get your cardio in. It’s in a fun area, too; Pizzeria Popolare, a great Italian restaurant, is just down the street, and you’re within easy exploring distance of all the boutiques and galleries the Marais has to offer.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, Bluetooth sound system, television, balcony, pets allowed

Best for: A small group of friends—who still want their own space.

We’d book this Airbnb for the tiles alone. From the rainbow-colored bathtub to the celery green kitchen to the traditional tomettes that run throughout, it’s an effortlessly charming spot, located on the third floor of an 18th-century building. The enviable design continues from the baby blue bedroom to the painted furniture; it’ll be more than obvious that you’re staying in one of the more creative, artistic quartiers of the city. (And if you want to get some of your own work done, the dedicated office area is happy to oblige.) While it’s in a bustling neighborhood, the apartment itself is at the back of the property, so you’ll have quiet when you need it.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathrooms; sleeps 3

Amenities: Bathtub, elevator, coffee maker, building staff

If you picked the Marais because of its art scene, you might as well commit to the experience and book an Airbnb directly overlooking the Picasso Museum. Sought-after location aside, this duplex feels welcoming from the moment you step in the door. Hexagonal terracotta tiles line the floor, a large dining table is the perfect spot for a cozy night in, and every nook and cranny is filled with glass vases and art. When you want to head out for dinner, you’re spoilt for choice—but start with Chez Nenesse, a classic, red-and-white checkered tablecloth bistrot, that’s just four minutes away.

Amenities: Kitchen, washer, Bose sound system, indoor fireplace, coffee maker

The first thing this Airbnb has going for it is its location: It’s situated right on the Île Saint-Louis, one of the city’s two islands, and therefore has a more quaint feel to it than some of the busier arrondissements. (Plus you’re just five minutes from Berthillon, the best ice cream in the area.) The second thing, of course, is its style. The building itself is listed as a historic monument dating back to the 17th century, and interior highlights like a painted ceiling and gilded mirror amplify the antique appeal. Even the piano area, a tiny nook off one of the bedrooms, has a blue marble floor and matching tile mural—it’s all extremely decadent.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, piano, indoor fireplace, parking, hot tub

We found your Parisian tree house. Tucked away near the busy Place des Vosges, the fourth-floor apartment is a calm respite, well-sized for a couple or solo traveler in search of more unique accommodation. Here, rustic wood beams accent nearly every ceiling and wall, textured brick flooring adds warmth, and a large, tiled tub looks out onto Haussmannian rooftops for a truly cozy stay. It even has two balconies—sure, they may be tiny, but the sweeping views of the city’s architecture more than makes up for their size.

Amenities: Washer, television, piano, balcony, bathtub

Best for: Those looking for a non-traditional vacation rental.

A bedroom adorned in pink toile de Jouy print, a working fireplace in the living room, a dining room that’s overflowing with plants and dressed up with a gilded mirror: this apartment, to borrow some first-level French, is très chic. It’s deceptively spacious—thanks to a sofa bed, it can actually sleep up to six people—making it ideal for a girls’ trip to the city. With a spacious living area and a well-equipped kitchen, it’s certainly designed to handle a larger group. A nice bonus? You’re within walking distance of the beloved bookstore Shakespeare and Company for a souvenir you can employ on the long flight home.

Amenities: Kitchen, TV, fireplace, washer/dryer, bathtub

Steps away from the bustling Odéon neighborhood and landmarks like the Pantheon and the Luxembourg Garden, this apartment is ideally situated for first-timers to the city of lights. With original 1930s features preserved and played up, it's also well-decorated: Art Deco details, like geometric borders, curved ceiling cut-outs, and arched doorways pop up throughout. (The turquoise bathtub nook is a particular highlight; the glass wall in the dining room is another.) This rental has tons of space for a family as well as several kid-friendly amenities available upon request; book it for a longer stay in the city.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, piano, Bluetooth sound system, exercise equipment, television, high chair, board games, elevator, parking, pets allowed

Location: By the Pantheon and the Luxembourg Garden

This literary, light-filled Airbnb is located in a building that houses several artists studios—notes of which can be found everywhere from the airy, industrial-style layout to the perfectly imperfect collection of decor to the multi-colored tiles in the kitchen. (As for the literary tie-in: Bookworms will appreciate the massive wall of books in the upstairs bedroom. Take your pick.) The home is mere blocks away from the Jardin du Luxembourg, in Montparnasse. Browse the aforementioned bookshelf and grab a paperback, pick up a coffee from one of the many cafés in the area, and take a morning to yourself in the gardens.

Amenities: Kitchen, washer/dryer, TV, crib, courtyard

Best for: Avid readers always looking for a new, picturesque spot to get lost in a book.

For the solo traveler who never wants to be too far from the sparkling lights of the Eiffel Tower, this little studio is a cozy cocoon just six minutes away. (Starting quite literally with the bed, which is cordoned off from the rest of the space by a chic glass wall and a gauzey curtain.) A tiny kitchenette stocked with all the essential appliances lets you make the most of local treats—helpful, as the famous Rue Cler street market is just around the corner, so you can stock up on cheeses, quiche, and even rotisserie chickens for quiet meals at home.

Amenities: Washer, elevator, pet-friendly, housekeeping available at a fee

Location: On Rue Amélie, a quick walk to the Eiffel Tower

It’ll be hard to beat this central location: This sunny, spacious two-bedroom is situated directly at the base of the Champ de Mars, the grassy park that houses the Eiffel Tower. It’s as stately as its zip code implies—think, period-appropriate wall moldings that reflect its 19th-century origins and oversized windows, with the occasional unexpected pop of color (like a yellow window in the kitchen and pistachio dining chairs) to keep it from feeling stuffy. It also comes with an espresso machine, so if you ever tire of your local boulangerie—unlikely—you can start the day with coffee at home.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathrooms; sleeps 3

Location: At the foot of the Eiffel Tower

Best for: Ticking the Eiffel Tower off your bucket list.

It’s conveniently located in the heart of Paris and stocked with modern creature comforts like a Nespresso machine and a Netflix-enabled television, but you really only need one reason to book this apartment: the massive terrace. Equipped with outdoor dining and seating, it’s a rare thing to find in the busy city (and, should you ever want a little quiet, an ideal spot to enjoy an apéro at home). Though it only has one proper bedroom, it can actually sleep four thanks to a sofa bed in the living room. For families looking for a comfortable spot near all the top sights, this is a great option.

Amenities: Washer, blackout shades, HDTV, Bose sound system, exercise equipment, travel crib, kitchen, Nespresso coffee maker, dishwasher, terrace, paid parking available

Best for: Travelers for whom a terrace with a view is a non-negotiable.

Staying in this palatial sixth-floor penthouse will feel like time travel—it sits within a historic Haussmann building and offers original details like 18th-century wood floors, hand-painted wallpaper, antique fireplaces, and a Napoleon-style oval room. It’s bourgeois luxury in every sense. The entire space enjoys plenty of light thanks to French windows opening onto three balconies, and amenities like a full kitchen and entry hall with a piano will make it difficult to venture outside (though you’ll want to—it’s in close proximity to some of Paris’s most coveted attractions like the Louvre, Opera Garnier, Champs Élysées).

Amenities: Washer/dryer, piano, kitchen, elevator, balcony, antique fireplaces

Best for: Anyone who knows what a “Napoleon-style oval room” is (interior design buffs, this one’s for you).

On the fifth floor of a traditional Haussmann building (there is an elevator, don’t worry) sits this elegant sunny spot. A long balcony stretches outside and includes a small bistro set for breakfasts outside—though the spacious dining room is also an enticing option. From the red-and-cream checkerboard kitchen to the ornate crown molding in the living area, it’s endlessly charming. Montmartre is only 15 minutes away; perhaps more importantly, depending on what your itinerary priorities are, the famous bakery Mamiche is an even-shorter 10 minute walk. (The brioche and the ham sandwich alone are good reasons to make a daily pilgrimage there each morning.)

Amenities: Bathtub, washer, sound system, board games, fire place, balcony, elevator

Best for: Design inspiration and proximity to an incredible bakery.

Originally belonging to the painter Georges Braque back in 1911, this sweet studio has since been re-done and can now fit up to four guests (the sofa converts to a bed, if you don’t mind a slightly crowded living space). The renovation didn’t strip it of its character, though, and between the primary-colored kitchen storage cubbies and the floor-to-ceiling windows that let the light stream in, it’s one of the more unique apartment rentals in Paris. The bay windows look out onto a courtyard, so you’ll have plenty of peace despite being located in one of the city’s most bustling areas for nightlife.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, kitchen, shared backyard, coffee maker, crib/travel crib/children’s books available upon request, balcony

Best for: Those hoping to experience the city’s artistic spirit beyond a visit to the Louvre.

Right below Pigalle on Rue Cadet, this quiet one-bedroom is surrounded by bakeries, cheese shops, and greengrocers. Everything you’d need is within walking distance; head to Racines, a hole-in-the-wall Italian spot with a decadent tiramisù, for a date night in the neighborhood. Inside, a fully equipped kitchen and multiple workspaces ensure you have all the essentials to stretch out and make this temporary spot feel like home. With sloping ceilings and views onto the city’s greyscale rooftops, it feels like the coziest attic—peaceful, personal, and chic enough to make you want to stay awhile.

Amenities: Washer, kitchen, dishwasher, coffee maker

If you can’t pick between the trendy 10th or 3rd arrondissements—don’t. This bright and airy one-bedroom is smack in the middle, in an ideal area full of hole-in-the-wall eateries and stylish spots to grab an apéro before a late dinner. Since it’s owned and designed by an architect, its interiors are especially appealing: The blend of vintage furniture and flourishing greenery might just inspire you to redecorate when you get home. In the meantime, you’ll feel right at home. The kitchen is big enough to whip up meals of your own, if you feel inspired—or at least, a quick breakfast before heading out for the day.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 1.5 bathrooms; sleeps 2

Amenities: Bathtub, washer, blackout shades, HDTV, Apple sound system, piano, kitchen, dishwasher, Nespresso coffee maker

Location: Right on the border of the 10th and the 3rd arrondissements

Best for: Bookmarking design inspiration.

Overlooking the rooftops of Paris, this small but well-appointed apartment (yes, it has an elevator) is perfect for a couple. From a zellige-tiled kitchen to a teeny balcony where you can sip a cocktail during golden hour, you’ll find everything you need for a short stint in the city. But the best part is, hands down, its location: The home is right by the Canal. Here, you’ll find a livelier, younger scene, with natural wine bars, trendy restaurants, and an atmosphere that feels decidedly removed from the touristy center. (Early June, a local-favorite restaurant and wine bar with a rotating cast of guest chefs, is a leisurely 15-minute walk away.)

Best for: Proximity to your new favorite wine bar.

For a vacation rental that feels designed by someone’s French grandma, choose this colorful, eclectic spot and make yourself at home. The kitchen, with its checkerboard-covered table, citron walls, and collected jumble of various tools and trinkets, is undoubtedly the center; but the bedrooms (there are three), with their massive windows and original terracotta floors are also nice—especially if you’re traveling with a big group, and want to make sure you each have enough space. When you do want to dine out, you’ll be well-positioned: Bistrot des Tournelles and Chez Paul, two wonderful traditional bistros, are located in this neighborhood.

Best for: Cosplaying Julia Child for the weekend.

Not all Parisian Airbnbs involve ornate crown moldings and baroque antiques; some, like this loft, can lean quite industrial. Iron beams and high ceilings make it seem even more spacious (the space itself is located in an old printing house); glass windows overlook an internal courtyard, if you need a quiet temporary home. Sandwiched between République and Canal St. Martin, it’s in a fun, more local part of the city. If it’s warm enough, walk along the water in the afternoon before ducking into Chambre Noir, a little wine bar near the apartment, for small plates and a crisp glass of white.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, TV, air conditioning, pet-friendly

Best for: Fans of industrial architecture.

This two-bedroom apartment may just house the best balcony in all of Paris. It’s well-furnished, with plenty of potted plants and a bistro set for taking your breakfast outside, weather-permitting, but the views of the Haussmann buildings and Eiffel Tower in the distance are what makes it really special. Inside, the design is cozy, with floral quilts and Art Deco-inspired lighting casting everything in a warm glow. Even the entrance to the apartment is special. While the fifth floor rental is accessible by elevator, you may just find yourself choosing to take the stairs, which are lined with stained glass windows.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, Sonos Bluetooth sound system, indoor fireplace, air conditioning, coffee maker, balcony, outdoor furniture, elevator

Perched in the heart of Montmartre in the hilly, cobblestone-lined streets of the Abbesses neighborhood, this one-bedroom home is ideal for the couple who likes their decor collected, full of personality, and a tiny bit mismatched. Starting with the mix of antique furnishings in the living room (including a red velvet armchair) and going right through to the lemon-yellow bedroom, the design of this place will make you feel like you’re visiting your artistic Parisian friend—no cold, white-box rooms here. When you do want to hit the tourist spots, the Basilica of Sacré Coeur is just a 15-minute walk away.

Best for: The eclectic traveler coming to Paris to peruse the flea markets.

You’re alone in Paris, and you need an inspiring studio from which to focus on your creative project (or just finish your book in peace): This artist’s loft is it. Tall ceilings and an oversized window create a light-filled environment, while a dedicated workspace offers a quiet place to concentrate. There’s a small but well-appointed kitchen so you can cook your meals at home and truly feel at ease during your stay, however long it may be.

Amenities: Washer, crib, coffee maker, shared backyard

Best for: Anyone coming to Paris to get out of a creative rut.

From the terracotta tomettes to the oversized windows, this sunny one-bedroom is perfect for the solo traveler or a couple. The building dates back to the 19th century, but the decor is firmly 21st: Butter yellow bedding and a mustard-striped kitchen skirt are design ideas to bookmark for when you get home. And you can’t trump the location: It’s right in the heart of Montmartre, only a few blocks away from Boulangerie Raphaëlle (one of the all-time best bakeries in the city—trust us).

Amenities: Travel crib available upon request, coffee maker

Jeans and ballerinas are the unofficial uniform of the city (and, conveniently, make a comfortable ensemble for a day of shopping). Bring an extra-large tote as your personal item on the plane so you have plenty of space to shuttle back all your souvenirs… including some French pharmacy goodies, of course.

After combing through hundreds of listings in a destination’s most desirable neighborhoods, we narrow down our list by reviewing a variety of determining factors, from the logistics of price, location, and amenities, to important details such as reviews and host information. From there, we take into consideration aesthetic details such as design, natural light, and overall look and feel of the home. The final edit is a well-rounded list that ensures booking a stay will result in a safe and stylish holiday.

#6889. Rift grows among Senate Democrats over who will lead in majority

Sens. Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin hold a news conference calling for a “bold direction” for Senate Democrats on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

More Democrats emerged Tuesday wanting someone besides Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., to lead their conference in the majority.

But Schumer maintained confidence he would be reelected to the post despite Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., publicly calling for a different leader or a “concrete plan” that provides change.

“I’m confident I will be elected majority leader, and our caucus is really united in focusing on bringing down costs, on ending the corruption, on ending the chaos, on ending the war,” Schumer told reporters Tuesday. “We have great unity in our caucus, and I’ll be proud to lead it.”

Sanders said during a news conference Tuesday the election was about “change and the need for the Democratic Party to move in a new and bold direction.”

“I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader,” Sanders said, calling for an “economy that works for all, not just the people on top.”

“Do I think Chuck has been leading in that direction?” he asked. “No.”

Some incoming members and now incumbents have pointed to Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen as one possibility to challenge Schumer. Van Hollen had previously thrown cold water on the idea by saying he was instead “kicking the tires” on a presidential run in 2028 but has recently changed his tune.

A person familiar with Van Hollen’s thinking said he “has received an outpouring of calls on running for majority leader and is now in active listening mode.”

Slotkin did not endorse anyone for leader but said she had a “really productive conversation” with Van Hollen yesterday.

“Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete plan that’s definitely different. I’m a ‘no’ until and unless I see that from anyone,” she said, urging her peers to “withhold quorum” when Senate Democrats hold their leadership elections “until you get that plan and you feel like you have a voice in that plan.”

She urged not just a roadmap for the first 100 days, but ideas for how to “communicate differently.” As for her own future, she said, “I am not actively seeking this job. I’m seeking change.”

Asked about his plans Monday evening, Van Hollen said, “It’s not about me, but I am listening to the thousands of people who have been calling for change, but especially listening to our members, with a particular ear to new members who have just come off the campaign trail.”

“What I’ve said from the very beginning is, we shouldn’t have a coronation. We should have a caucus discussion about what we're going to do with the power and responsibilities that have been invested in us,” Van Hollen said. “I’m in listening mode and haven’t shut the door.”

Van Hollen took it a step further at an event Tuesday in Washington, D.C., criticizing the minority leader and Democrats’ campaign arm over their preferences in some primaries. “Schumer and the DSCC sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC against these candidates,” he said, according to a livestream of the event.

Schumer tried to tamp down the suggestion of a rivalry. “We talk frequently, and we’re united — united in lowering costs, and united in ending this damn war,” he said of Van Hollen.

Others threw their support behind Schumer ahead of the Democratic leadership elections, which are expected to take place in December.

Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., praised Schumer for raising money and recruiting candidates like Sens.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio and Roy Cooper of North Carolina to help land at minimum seven seats, and potentially nine if Alaska and Mississippi ultimately swing their way.

“That takes vision. It takes clarity of thought. It takes strategic leadership, and that is what Sen. Schumer has done. And that is why you will see, despite all grumblings, enormous gratitude,” she said.

Gillibrand pointed to candidates like Scott Colom, the Democrat in Mississippi who is currently leading GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a nail-biter of a race. “That wave doesn’t get created by magic. It gets created by hard work and putting the pieces together over years,” she said.

Colom, however, has been noncommittal, telling MS NOW, “Too many of our leaders are from the same areas of the country,” pointing to the Brooklyn roots of both Schumer and current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to run for speaker on the House side.

Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., said he and Schumer have had their differences. But he implied he backs him for majority leader: “At the end of the day, these are historic numbers. It’s time for us to unify. We are going to work together as a caucus to plan together about how to move forward for what the country wants us to do, and I think we have the person who I think is going to lead us there.”

Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., said Democrats have “an opportunity to do things differently, and I think we will, regardless of who the leader is. It doesn’t really matter whose name is on the door.”

“Yes,” he said of his support for Schumer, noting that so far, nobody has officially stepped up to the plate. “This is a guy that worked incredibly hard over the last couple of years. I know people have other opinions about this. But we have a mandate to do things and get things done for the American people.”

Mark Schoeff Jr., Paul M. Krawzak and Kelly Livingston contributed to this report.

Cozy, polished pairs to wear all winter long.

There’s a reason shearling keeps coming back every cold season. It’s the rare material that manages to be cozy and stylish at once, with a plush, cloud-like lining that wraps your feet in warmth and a rich texture that instantly makes an outfit feel more intentional. What began as practical gear for sheepherders and pilots has become a fixture of modern closets, showing up on everything from chic boots to sleek slippers, ballet flats, and fashion-forward sneakers.

Part of its staying power is function. Shearling is naturally insulating, breathable, and moisture-wicking, so your feet stay warm without overheating. Versatility is another reason why shearling has become so popular. The same material that elevates a pair of jeans and a sweater on a weekend errand run can make lounging at home feel like a small luxury.

Whether you’re hunting for the perfect slip-on to kick off at the door, a boot to carry you through winter, or a statement piece that turns heads, below are the must-have shearling shoes that earn a spot in your rotation this season.

#6884. Why Don’t You … Take Fashion Inspiration from the World’s Great Performers?

Diana Vreeland had a singular take on not only fashion but life. Her eccentricity has become folklore and was best exemplified in an illustrated column of irreverent advice for chic living she called “Why Don’t You?” Resurrected and reimagined for modern life, the column, now written by Bazaar’s executive digital director, Lynette Nylander, will dispense tips on how to live stylishly, decadently, and daringly.

Here’s a thought: Don’t get dressed. Mount a production. Put on a show. Go on tour. And if the reviews are lukewarm, don’t change the costume; blame the critic! For the performance issue, Lynette Nylander takes cues from the stage’s most stylish to arm you with tips for stepping out.

that the “effortless” look took 40 minutes. The “I just threw it on” leather jacket, the smudged eye makeup, the shirt that looks slept in: All of it is stagecraft. Miley Cyrus’s new rock-star look personifies this. She’s not someone to shy away from an “era,” and this one is all tousled hair, loads of lashes, and leather and lace from the likes of Tom Ford, Roberto Cavalli, and Saint Laurent. Effortless? No. Fabulous? Absolutely!

some noise. Taffeta rustles, silk whispers, embellishments jangle, and leather creaks with intent. Performance is not only visual. The swish of a skirt on a staircase is part of the entrance, and the weight of crepe hugging the hips is part of the walk. The late, great Tina Turner was a master of clothes that created a symphony as she writhed around the stage; often, they were the creations of the late, great Bob Mackie. Björk went viral earlier this year at the Venice Biennale in a neon-pink Bottega Veneta dress made of fiberglass shards that jingle-jangled together as she fist-pumped. The lesson? Dress for the ear as well as the eye.

the precision of a uniform. The chef’s whites, the lawyer’s suit, the professor’s tweeds, the tailored black of the gallery assistant: Each is a costume designed with a very particular audience in mind. Even people who wear the same thing every day are making a statement, and the strongest of them curate that repetition with real rigor. Consistency, done well, is a kind of theater. Just don’t make it boring! Consider Steve Jobs, who famously wore only Issey Miyake turtlenecks and Levi’s. Truly the only tech titan to ever have taste!

the art of quick change. For Céline Dion’s fall residency at the Plénitude Arena in Paris, underneath the spotlight wasn’t the only site where a performance took place. Like all true divas, Dion knows that every moment of every day is an opportunity to perform. Outside of the Royal Monceau hotel, her home in Paris, where her faithful fans lined up to greet her, she treated onlookers to a dance, a song, an air-kiss, and always a fashion show: off-the-runway looks from Jacquemus, Loewe, and Phoebe Philo. As they say, all the world’s a stage.

the ordinary garment its moment. Not every act needs sequins. A perfect white tee, a pair of jeans that have taken on the shape of a life, a forever leather jacket worn with confidence: these are the understudies who steal the show. Performance in fashion is not always about drama. Sometimes it is the quiet authority of a simple thing worn exactly right. A disciple of this way of dressing? #6883. How to Grow a Beard

So you want to learn how to grow a beard. First off, you should know that it helps to have the right genetics. Second, you have to stay committed to the endeavor. Too often, beard-growing attempts end before they’ve even had a chance to establish itself.

“I’d say give it at least three to four weeks of solid growth before you even think about touching it with clippers,” Victor Mendoza, co-founder of beard care brand Viking Revolution, says. “Your beard needs time to actually show you what it’s going to look like, and that growth period lets you see the natural direction everything’s growing in. Plus, some hairs take longer to come in than others, so patience is key.”

There’s a sweet spot between letting your facial hair grow out and knowing when it’s time to take the trimmers for the best results possible, even if you can’t go full lumberjack. These are the best tips to maximize your hair follicles’ potential whether this is your first beard or your fiftieth.

There are many different beard styles to choose from; you don’t need to stick to neatly manicured, uniform look. Let your growth be influenced by the style you want to achieve.

“Your genes determine hair thickness, growth rate, density, and color,” Mendoza says. “If your dad or granddad had a thin beard, you’re probably dealing with the same hand, and that’s just life.”

If your beard is patchy, or if it has a unique growth pattern (sparse on the cheeks, full on the goatee, for example), then you should set your expectations properly. This goes for beards big, small, and medium alike. And while nutrition is important for hair growth, you can’t cheat genetics with your diet.

Patience is a virtue. Not only can a little time help fill in some patchiness, but it’s also requisite for almost any style. A beard transforms into something new every week. So, if it’s seeming like you’ll never reach your goal—in particular if it’s a long beard—then you honestly might wake up one morning and realize that you’ve arrived at the destination.

Mendoza says to wait at least two weeks before you start to do a cleanup, but only around the ends, i.e. the hairs that aren’t within the perimeter in which you want your beard to grow. That’ll help you figure out your beard’s natural shape.

One of the tenets of beard maintenance is to keep it defined. In short: shave the neckline and clean up the cheek lines. These keep it more beard-like and less neckbeard-like—unless, for some reason, a wooly stoner beard is your aim. In that case, let it grow wild and free.

The second way to keep things looking intentional is to sculpt and trim your beard as it grows. It might feel counterproductive—and counter to #2—but it’s the same way you need to get haircuts while growing out your hair. As Mendoza says, this helps direct the hair exactly where it needs to be: Fuller in some spots, less so in others. The styling products in the next tip can of course help influence things, but you foremost want to keep hairs in check as needed: This can mean spot-checking strays, snipping away split ends, or simply taking out some bulk. You’ll want a beard trimmer or a sharp pair of scissors.

There are a handful of beard products you should consider picking up if you’re serious about proper care and maintenance. A few drops of beard oil will absorb quickly and give your hair the right nutrients (plus a pinch of shine), while also making it less wild and frizzy. You can also swap in a beard balm or cream, something slightly heftier than an oil, to help style the beard and keep it in place all day. What’s important is that you clean your beard every day with an actual beard wash and not just a regular shampoo, which Mendoza says will dry out your beard and your face.

Weekly maintenance will consist of a deep condition, which you can do in the shower. “If you’re doing those things consistently, your beard is going to look way healthier and fuller than most guys out there,” he says.

Beard brushes help exfoliate the skin beneath the beard, for starters, which lifts dead skin cells and prevents future flaking. Moreover, brushing your beard at the end of each day will ensure its health and tame-ability in the long haul. This distributes the natural oils produced in the skin, which otherwise collect at the base of the shaft and only nourish the bottom of each hair. This oil distribution prevents breakage, frizzing, and split ends. (This is a great time to apply a few drops of beard oil as a booster, especially after a shower.)

Once your base has grown out—this can take months—it’s time to really make it yours. One of our favorites is to snip the bridge between the mustache and the chin, thus marooning the mustache. Or, pare back the beard itself, leaving a fuller mustache. You have lots of options, and it’s your privilege as a beard grower to flaunt it.

#6882. The Hottest Thing in Nordic Design Right Now? The Vikings

Norway is a country built on craftsmanship.

Some of the earliest, most revered pioneers of craft and international trade in the country were the Vikings, who, between the 8th and 11th centuries, used wood, iron, and bone to create their post-and-beam longhouses, weapons, and ships. (Not to mention wool, linen, and leather for their unheralded colorful attire.)

Today, as interest in Viking culture outside of Norway and Scandinavia experiences an uptick thanks to pop culture, social media, and even sports, creatives in Norway are using the opportunity to introduce a new wave of curious travelers to Viking history through artisanal clothing, metalwork, and interior design steeped in this early culture.

Traditional wool weaving at Viking Valley.

“Travelers are more interested in Viking culture than ever,” says Torill Hylland, chair of Viking Valley. Even though this Gudvangen-located recreation village debuted a decade ago, Hylland witnessed a recent surge in visitors following this past summer’s FIFA World Cup, where Norway’s Erling Haaland popularized the Viking row as one of the catchiest celebrations of the football tournament.

“We've seen significant growth in interest in Norway,” adds Nelson Oliveira, managing director, Nordics for luxury travel operator Abercrombie & Kent. Launched in 2024, their small group trip itineraries include a visit to the Viking Valley where guests interact with the Viking chieftain, dine in the reindeer-clad, candle-lit dining hall and visit the resident blacksmith, who continues to supply ironworks for the community, including door hinges and locks. “The Viking era is such an important part of Norway’s history, and we wanted to give guests an opportunity to experience that heritage beyond simply visiting a museum,” says Oliveira.

Outside the village, quotidian Viking-inspired design is flourishing—and notably predates Haaland’s viral row chant. Matilde Brandt, marketing manager of Klesarven, a Viking heritage clothing retailer founded in 2015 by Lene Lorentzen, credits the global interest in historybounding—where elements of historical fashion are incorporated into everyday styles—for the spike in popularity of their Viking-inspired styles.

“There is so much more to the [Viking] story than bearded men fighting and wearing dark colors,” says Brandt. Inspired by Hollywood’s enduringly maligned, inaccurate depictions of Viking Age Scandinavia, Klesarven focuses on historically accurate representations of the people living during that age. “Most of them were farmers, fishermen and craftspeople [who] wore bright, colorful clothing and were well put together,” says Brandt.

A Klesarven Frøya linen dress and Favn shawl.

These motifs are realized across Klesarven’s collection of wool sweaters, linen shirts, and riding skirts. One of Klesarven’s most popular designs is the Viking Age apron dress, inspired by a garment reserved for special occasions and ornamented with colorful beads, brooches, and jewelry crafted from silver, gold, and bronze. Women were also buried in these garments. “It keeps history alive,” says Brandt. “In this way, we help preserve old techniques and craftsmanship.”

Preserving heritage is also a motivation of Runestone’s founders, Sonya and Kim Andre. Having both grown up on a stretch of coastline dotted with Viking history—Sonya from Uddevalla on Sweden’s west coast and her husband, Kim, from Halden, just across the Norwegian border—Runestone was born from a personal “obsession” with Viking culture.

When the couple began building an online outfitter dedicated to Viking apparel, Norse jewelry, and rune wall art (the alphabet of Viking culture), Sonya recognized the bigger drive: “A lot of the brands out there lean into that ‘dressed up as a Viking’ look,” says Sonya. Runestone promises the opposite; born as a way to embrace history through a modern lens with designs, symbols, and styles as “something anyone can wear and connect with, not just a costume,” says Sonya.

“Every design has a real story behind it—a god, a creature, a rune, and we care a lot about getting that story right,” Sonya continues. “We’re carrying forward the spirit of the Vikings more than the actual lifestyle, religion, or the more brutal parts of the history.”

Every week, Sonya receives emails, primarily from younger folks who are responding to the uptick in social media attention surrounding Viking culture. “They’re asking really specific questions,” she says, like inquiring about the gods—especially Odin, who is widely regarded as the god of wisdom and warfare—and requesting that Sonya point them toward reliable sources instead of pop culture tales.

For the curious travelers who make it to Norway, they have more opportunity than ever to engage with Viking heritage, from active opportunities like Viking Valley and shopping at Klesarven to passive participation at hotels.

In the northwestern Ålesund region, Storfjord Hotel was built in traditional Norwegian laft style with timber logs and turf roofs (the latter prioritized in Viking times for insulation). On Manshausen Island, located off the coast of northern Norway, the restaurant walls at the eponymous resort are covered with overlapping wooden scales built in the traditional Viking construction. Its groundskeeper team consists of two dozen sheep—an ancient Nordic breed that was kept during the Viking era.

“A hotel can become much more than a beautiful place to stay,” says Linda Gram Egede-Nissen, co-owner and CEO of interior design firm Gathe + Gram. “It can offer guests a subtle introduction to the culture and history of its surroundings.” In Trondheim, the northern city which served as the Viking capital of Norway many centuries ago, Gathe + Gram just completed the design blueprint for Eras, a boutique hotel where every room has its own distinctive name and story rooted in Viking history, mythology, or craftsmanship.

For this project, Gram Egede-Nissen was “particularly fascinated” by the “remarkable precision, complexity and beauty in the detailing” of historic jewelry from the Viking era. Her team translated the shapes, patterns, and proportions of spenne (buckles), skålspenne (ornamental brooches), and polyedrisk (beads) into architectural details and smaller design elements—decorative cushions, sculptural chandeliers, and wall art—throughout the interiors. “There is an incredible richness in the [Viking-era] jewelry—and many of these forms feel surprisingly relevant even today,” says Gram Egede-Nissen.

“To me, that is where heritage becomes truly relevant,” adds Gram Egede-Nissen. “Not when we preserve it as something untouchable, but when we allow it to inspire new ideas.”

#6879. How to Play GTA VI All Weekend Without Destroying Your Body

The day has finally arrived. Grand Theft Auto VI is here, and you’ve taken that “sick day” to cause chaos on the streets of Vice City. After more than 10 years of waiting, you’re finally back in one of the franchise’s most classic locations, this time with an open world to explore. It’s not hyperbole to call this the most highly anticipated game in history. With more than 17 million preorders, that’s a lot of people who will be running from the police while trying to avoid (or rack up) six stars.

If you’re one of the many fans who’ve cleared out their schedule to binge the game this weekend, you’ll want to make sure you emerge from your haze with extremities that still function.

“The metaphor we like to share with pro players or casual gamers is the concept of the health bar,” says Dr. Matthew Hwu, owner of physical therapy clinic 1 Health Point in Monrovia, California. “The muscles and tendons of your wrist, hand, thumb, as you move the analog stick, only have so much capacity or ‘max HP’ that they can handle throughout the day.”

Below, we spoke with Dr. Hwu and other veteran gamers about how to keep your “HP” bar full for your whole weekend without developing carpal tunnel.

Playing a game for long hours puts the soft tissues in your hands and arms into overdrive. When you ramp things up, you’ll feel sore and fatigued. The most common version of this is “tendon-based problems of the wrist and hand,” says Dr. Hwu, who has spent more than 11 years working with e-sports players to help them recover from injuries. As GTA VI will be available on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series S and X, most people will be using a controller, which puts the thumbs under a lot of stress as people “control the analog stick to flip left, up, right, down; press A, B, X, Y.” The most common gaming injuries are gamer’s thumb and tennis elbow, according to the Cleveland Clinic.

So, don’t forget to take breaks. Dr. Hwu recommends at least a five-minute break for every 90 minutes played, though younger players are more resilient. If you want to push it, the key is taking longer breaks afterwards. “Two hours, 10-minute break, three hours, 15-minute break,” Dr. Hwu says. “If you want to be degenerate, you can be a smart degen.” You can also be strategic about scheduling more downtime after sequences with higher APM (actions per minute), that are more intensive on hand muscles. In essence, go touch grass after a high-stakes bank robbery.

That said, after more than a decade of waiting for what our reviewer described as “the most technically and artistically impressive game world ever made,” your instinct may be to lock in. So it’s wise to plan for breaks ahead of time. Set alarms on your phone or watch. If one goes off in the middle of a mission, commit to taking a break after crashing that helicopter. Make sure you eat and stay hydrated, and move your body, whether that’s a neighborhood walk or just a short twirl around your apartment before your next mission.

“It’s basically just your muscle and tendon tissue recovery, it’ll restore a little bit of HP over time,” Dr. Hwu says. “When you go out and walk outdoors, that can help with your overall circulation, nervous system as well. So you don’t feel like that meme where you come out of the cave and you’re like a ghost.”

Just like in other forms of training, stretching is a key part of your self-care arsenal for long hours of gaming. To loosen up for a long stretch of car-hijacking, do a few stretches before turning on your console, and during cut scenes. Your body will tell you what areas feel tight and could use some attention. But don’t forget those thumb muscles. “Bring your thumb away from the next finger, stretching it down,” Dr. Hwu says. “Every time you’re flicking back, left, or right, you might be using these muscles.”

You’ll also want to stretch your index fingers after long hours of beating ass with a crowbar while riding your motorcycle. “Every time you press your trigger,” Dr. Hwu says, “you’re using the extensors, the top side of your fingers, but also the flexors to push down.” You can also work on relaxing your forearm muscles, by extending your arm out and pushing your palm downward.

After 13 years, and a budget rumored to rival that of Dubai’s Burj Khalifa skyscraper, the new Grand Theft Auto is finally here. Our critic's verdict? It's a tour de force that reimagines what a video game can be.

Don’t forget your neck and upper back, which can feel stiff from holding onto stress after high speed chases and parachute combat. It’s so easy to load tension onto those upper traps as you shrimp further into your recliner while bird watching, or scoring a pair of black half-rim sunglasses and Eris sneakers (definitely not Nikes) for Jason (no judgment here).

“I will do small things: roll my neck from side to side, stretch my traps by sitting on one hand and pulling my head [in the] opposite direction,” Calliope Ryder, platform director at GYLD, previously a producer on Tales of the Shire, says. “[I] tense my calves in spurts to help with blood flow, or stand up and let my body fold at the hips while swaying side to side with my arms crossed. Again, alerts to remind me to do it are necessary or I'll go hours without noticing.”

Meanwhile, using a heating pad or an ice pack on a sore area (like your lower back) can help with any nagging dull pain you’re feeling. Heat loosens up stiff muscles, while ice can help dull the achy sensation. They won’t build your long-term strength, but they’ll make you feel better in the moment.

If you’re old enough for back pain, then you’re old enough to have to consider video game ergonomics. Wherever you’re gaming, Dr. Hwu’s recommendation is simple: Sit with your legs at a 90-degree angle, feet planted on the ground, back appropriately supported. Then put a pillow on your lap and rest your arms on it. This helps prevent forearm strain and hunching over. You can even haul your expensive Aeron from your office into the living room, rather than rotting on the sofa and ruining your back.

There are also a number of helpful gaming peripherals. Maddy Myers, editor in chief and co-founder of video game publication Mothership, uses a specific gaming pillow from a brand called Mechanism. “The pillow allows you to have the handheld device suspended in the air in a comfortable, adjustable spot so that you don’t tire out your arms from holding it up,” she says. “You can also put a controller on there.”

Using the device helps her get through play stretches of eight hours a day on the weekends, “while taking breaks to eat, do chores, stretch.” It’s been especially invaluable during high-intensity work periods. “I have to play GTA 6 for my job, so I am really going to be relying on these tools to keep my arms and body feeling as close to normal as possible,” she says.

Don’t let a terribly designed controller be the reason you develop carpal tunnel. Julia Lee, section lead for video game guides at Polygon, plays at least two hours of games a day, and will sometimes fit in 10-hour sessions. Her wrists started hurting and “those flat [Nintendo Switch] Joy-Cons were directly to blame,” she says. “I ended up getting a Nintendo Switch Pro Controller (which has a much more ergonomic shape and grip), and that helped alleviate pain a lot.” She also reminds herself not to hold the controller so tight, as it causes pain.

As Dr. Hwu explains, some controllers have staggered sticks, while others have an inline design. It all comes down to individual comfort and muscular endurance. He’s helped pro Call of Duty players modify their analog sticks, and has coached people to avoid death-gripping the controller. “If you use a claw grip position, an awkward grip, or a modded controller, that might lead to more stress for certain muscles in your wrist and hand,” he says.

If your hands are really killing you, there’s also the option of switching to another controller style altogether. “Moving two to four of my most awkward hand-based actions from my hands to my feet allows me to play longer,” John Warren, chief marketing officer and cofounder of Glydr, a foot-based video game controller, says. Warren has minicore disease, which causes muscle weakness. “Anytime you have an opportunity to stop overloading your hands while you play, you give your hands a little reprieve,” he says, “it makes your high-precision hand actions more accurate.”

Lastly, if you have existing injuries, and your medical provider has prescribed a brace, actually follow their guidance for how and when to use it. For my part, I use thumb braces called the Push Metagrips, to help support my floppy thumb joints anytime I plan on playing video games for long stretches.

So you’ve done all this work to binge GTA 6, and you’re feeling solid but a little sore. But you want to play for longer periods, snipe with greater accuracy, and fuck around with less fatigue. Consider going to the gym.

Doing exercises for those small muscles and tendons can help you build up that tolerance, like any other form of weight and endurance training. “When you rest, ice, massage, kinesio tape, you know, passive interventions, bracing, all of these things can restore your HP,” Dr. Hwu says. “It does nothing to change the size of your health bar, which represents the tissue’s capacity or your endurance. The way we do that is you can do specific exercises to build up or create a buffer for how much you’re going to handle.”

For any chronic pain, injuries, or conditions, it’s important to work with a physical therapist. I’m currently working with one for repetitive stress injury recovery, and doing exercises specific to playing video games. I do slow wrist curls with a two-pound weight, rotator cuff exercises with a resistance band, and squeeze an egg-shaped stress ball for thumb and forearm endurance. I also train my shoulders and core.

For those who aren’t managing any injuries, training those finger and arm muscles make it easier to game for longer periods. Consistency is key, and so is having reasonable expectations. Dr. Hwu recommends starting once a day, three to four times a week, “on a day where you’re not doing a lot, and then you’ll learn how your body responds to doing exercises within the context of your specific life, and you can make modifications to scale up the aggressiveness or scale down,” he says. As for seeing progress, “it takes four to six weeks for muscles, eight weeks for tendons.”

And don’t forget the stabilizer muscles in your shoulders, which hold up your upper body and support your arms. “I focus on ‘chest opening’ exercises that strengthen your back,” Ryder says. “I tend towards curving forward so I consciously strengthen the 'opposite' muscles so they pull my shoulders back a bit.” She also does chin tucks, to strengthen her deep neck flexors.

Strength training is also a great way to tackle back pain, another common complaint after gaming for hours. “A few years ago I started having extreme back pain when I sat in my office chair,” Gita Jackson, cofounder of video game publication Aftermath, says. They play one to two hours of games a day, but often play marathon sessions when new games come out. “The pain was excruciating, and sometimes my legs would get so stiff I couldn’t walk. Recovery started with physical therapy, and then a new ergonomic chair,” and now they regularly attend pilates.

“I really had no idea that if I wanted to continue playing noodley strategy games without pain that I would have to be a person who works out multiple times a week,” they say.

Maybe you’ve done a little too much, and your arms start to feel heavy as bricks, with thumbs that ache for hours. Even with the best precautions in place, it can happen to any of us.

“If it gets to a point where cumulatively, over days, symptoms are getting worse, maybe reflect and identify what you could change,” Dr. Hwu says. “If things are consistently sharp, or you start to feel some weakness, where when you go and try to pick up something, you’ll want to drop it. That’s a sign that it may be time to make a change in some of the variables that you can control.”

In 2002, weeks before the release of Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, the journalist David Kushner met Sam and Dan Houser, plus Rockstar co-founder Terry Donovan, at their SoHo loft. It would be their last and only in-depth sit-down before they decided that the world’s most successful video game required little explanation.

This is when paying attention to your daily habits is key. Instead of freaking out over hand pain, and deciding you need to quit playing cold turkey, you can instead think about what you did during the day that might have contributed to your discomfort. “How much you’re playing, what intensity you’re playing, are you taking breaks, are you exercising, how are you responding to the pain?” Dr. Hwu says. These are all factors in why you might be having pain, and all things to consider modifying. If it truly is tendon fatigue, then the key is finding the right volume of use, rather than quitting altogether.

There are also some signs to look out for that may require medical intervention. Dr. Hwu pointed me to 1 Health Point’s website, which suggests seeking a doctor’s opinion if your wrist looks swollen or bruised, if you can’t move or bear any weight, if your symptoms worsen or spread with rest, or if you experience constant hand numbness, especially if it comes with weakness.

Gaming for long hours ultimately comes down to using your common sense alongside your precious free will. Pay attention to your habits. Commit to taking breaks and stretching between bank robberies and doomscrolling through Snapmatic (in-game social media). Do some preventative exercises while planning out your next mission—with a soundtrack that includes Bad Bunny and Dua Lipa, as well as some ’80s bangers, you’ve already got the music for it. Your hands and arms will thank you, even if the regular people of Leonida probably won’t.

#6874. All the Details on Hailey Bieber’s Viral Blue K-Beauty Sheet Mask

The soothing mask is packed with PDRN, blue azulene, and mucin—and it’s coming to Amazon soon.

Hailey Bieber does not play about her skin care. The Rhode Skin founder recently posted a now-viral Instagram carousel showing the many masks she uses to treat her skin. Among the mix of traditional sheet masks, LED devices, rubber masks, and traditional creams was one standout—a blue sheet mask that has sent the internet down a rabbit hole. But of course we’re skin care sleuths, and we gathered all the details, including its benefits and where to buy it.

Jennifer Seo, head concierge at Aneue, a bespoke beauty and wellness travel concierge, immediately ID’d the mask and knows the brand well. She tells ELLE the mask is from Korean skin care brand Pyderin and that its PDRN Lift Cream is the most reordered product among her clients.

Bieber is wearing the Pyderin Hydrovuster PDRN SOS Hyal Soothing Mask, which is part of the brand’s Hydrovuster line. Seo says the lineup was developed as a hydrating, calming collection to soothe post-treatment skin or sensitive, reactive skin. The blue tint isn’t just for aesthetic purposes either; it comes from blue azulene, an anti-inflammatory and calming ingredient that also reduces redness. Dr. Chang Son, a board-certified dermatologist based in NYC, says that its main benefit is hydration. “There may also be an immediate soothing benefit, particularly for skin following sun exposure or experiencing irritation, along with a potential instant cooling effect that leaves the skin feeling refreshed and comforted,” Son explains.

What sets this mask apart from other sheet masks is that it’s soaked in a pharmaceutical-grade serum packed with PDRN in its highest purity. “[The treatment] is highly concentrated and synergizes well with blue azulene and mucin to heal and soothe the skin,” says Seo. The mask uses domestic PDRN extracted from Korean salmon, versus other brands that may use internationally sourced PDRN not from salmon, but from other types of fish, and may contain contaminants. “We have seen other sources of PDRN versus the raw PDRN that is used in Pyderin’s products, and there is a difference in the texture, scent, and color of this active ingredient,” Seo notes.

Son adds that the sodium PDRN used in this mask is more water-soluble, making it better suited for topical applications and easier to incorporate into skin care products such as creams and sheet masks. “Its primary role in topical formulations is hydration, although it is generally not considered as biologically active as injectable forms of PDRN,” says Son.

In addition to its purity, Pyderin uses a 99 percent pure source of PDRN that is also a small enough size, at 97 kilodaltons, to penetrate the skin. “If the particle size is too large, the ingredient will merely sit on top of the skin, whereas this PDRN product will penetrate the epidermis,” Seo explains.

Son and Seo agree that the combo of pure PDRN and blue azulene can be used regularly and is suitable for all skin types and skin tones, especially after skin treatments when skin can be sensitive or irritated. “I think it would be most beneficial for patients with chronic dry or inflamed skin like rosacea,” Son notes. “I generally do not recommend facial masks for patients with conditions involving significant epidermal barrier damage, such as severe eczema or cystic acne, as these may further irritate compromised skin.”

The mask is currently sold out, but according to a Pyderin IG post, it’ll be available via Amazon in mid-to-late November, so any day now.

#6871. How The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping Showcases Effie Trinket’s Fashion Evolution

Costume designer Bina Daigeler shares the inspiration behind the fashion in the new film.

If you follow red carpet fashion, these past few weeks, it’s been impossible to ignore Elle Fanning’s method dressing madness as Effie Trinket. From toy ballerina music box headpieces by Robert Wun fit for a fairy tale to makeup compact dresses (and matching headwear) from Givenchy, the fashion story is strong. All roads lead back to her character as young Effie Trinket from The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, which is making its theater debut on November 20. Based on Suzanne Collins’s 2025 novel of the same name, it is set 24 years before The Hunger Games and 40 years after The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes. It begins the morning of the 50th Hunger Games, with a 16-year-old Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) and Effie Trinket as a young stylist in the Capitol.

Bina Daigeler is the costume designer behind the new film, and with her team, she oversaw the creation of every single outfit from scratch, with a few helping accessories pulled from vintage specialists. She began with a mood board that focused on the aesthetic differences between the 13 districts while keeping in mind the personalities of the actors. Drusilla Sickle (Glenn Close) had a devoted board full of Alexander McQueen, John Galliano, and Vivienne Westwood, for instance. “It was really like old couture fashion,” Daigeler tells ELLE. “But pieces that, for me, would age very well, you know, that would keep up in time, because I think that is very important when you work on such a famous franchise; that you design for the future. That it’s still interesting in 10 years.”

“Working with Glenn Close, she really came to me and said, ‘I need to find a thread through all the costumes that are made for me, so that I can understand it,’” says Daigeler. “That was super important for her.” Daigeler wove everything together with “cool accessories to give her the strength,” and one very special finale look. “She wanted to have a big finale, you know, like a finale where she really feels like ‘I’m the winner. it’s nothing about Haymitch, it's all about me.’” Think: lots of red.

Daigeler also referenced Woodstock, Studio 54, the late ’60s and early ’70s. “I tried really to have a strong concept that has to do with the personality of each character,” she says. Unsurprisingly, given Effie Trinket’s predilection for fashion as a stylist, she was a big focus for Daigeler. “For example, young Effie Trinket, how did she become the Effie Trinket that Elizabeth Banks was? Here she is younger, she is fresh, she doesn’t have a lot of money or a fashion background. So it must be something that looked a little bit vintage that could be done at home, a mixture of fabrics, of textures, of color, something very young and fresh and fun.”

Early on in the film, we see Effie Trinket’s fashion as improvisational. But Daigeler intentionally showcases her ascension from fashion fan to fashion icon throughout the film. Daigeler says that Effie’s outfits all had to have fun elements. “The black kimono with the flowers and patchwork little waistcoat with a flowery blouse and all the color combinations were very strange, but it worked together,” she says. She also mentions her blue denim, Vivienne Westwood-inspired piece with huge sleeves as being the epitome of young Effie Trinket style.

“The most important thing was, for Effie, that she looks fun, but also free, because she is in the Capitol, but is still the freest and the most positive and optimistic character,” says Daigeler. “She doesn’t look like damaged and depressed and she had to come in and cheer them up and she definitely came with a solution. Our heroes somehow could trust her and they were so happy to see her. All the other characters from the Capitol, you really don’t know who you can trust.” Therefore, their aesthetic is darker while Effie is lighter and brighter.

Look out for the fashion Easter eggs throughout the film, like Effie Trinket’s butterfly crystal rings, which were just some of the pieces that Daigeler sourced vintage from one of her favorite specialists from around the world. Elsewhere, Haymitch has his own fashion revolution in a quieter way. “The way also how Haymitch wears the clothes and how they were aged and the colors, everything just comes together,” says Daigeler. “I think the audience will find, or I hope, that they find that there are things that resemble and they recognize it.”

Likewise for Caesar Flickerman (Kieran Culkin), the longtime Capitol television host, there’s an emphasis on fashionable suits. “It was very, very important that he can move because he is a very physical actor whom moves a lot, so he needed space in his suits,” says Daigeler. “Suits also had to give him power.”

And for Snow (Ralph Fiennes), too, suiting is used to convey power. “He’s very particular about fabrics, about the cut. So I went to a tailor in London, who I have known for many, many years,” she says. “Snow’s suits we developed really like a little bit, World War II military cuts, with a very strong shoulder and a very strong silhouette and these heavy fabrics, and the right colors. But then we gave him the fantasy through hand-embroidered lapels. It had also the hint to his rose that he always wears, and he has somehow always loved flowers.”

Fashion is both spectacle and a survival tool in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping. The odds are forever in fashion’s favor.
